value: In the AI Risk Management Framework, how is harmful bias linked to fairness?
reason: The Framework never defines harmful bias, so a 'what is' front promises a definition the back cannot give.

value: Fairness in AI includes addressing issues such as harmful bias and discrimination; the trustworthy characteristic is “fair – with harmful bias managed”.
reason: The old back was circular, and its 'must address' overstated the source: 'Fairness in AI includes concerns for equality and equity by addressing issues such as harmful bias and discrimination' (AI 100-1, PDF p. 22).

value: Managing harmful bias is only part of fairness: the Framework notes that systems in which harmful biases are mitigated are not necessarily fair.
reason: The old explanation repeated the back. The new one says why managing bias is not the whole story: 'Systems in which harmful biases are mitigated are not necessarily fair' (AI 100-1, PDF p. 22).

value: A is wrong because “satisfied” needs the assessment objective to be met, and an unrecorded claim does not show that. C is wrong because Special Publication 800-53A has only two findings, satisfied and other than satisfied. B is wrong because each determination statement produces one of those two findings.
reason: The findings come from each determination statement, not from each assessment procedure: 'Each determination statement contained within an assessment procedure executed by an assessor produces one of the following findings' (SP 800-53A, PDF p. 42).

value: A is wrong because all controls, particularly nontechnical ones, still need periodic assessment. B is wrong because training is itself a security control, covered by the Awareness and Training family of Special Publication 800-53. D is wrong because dashboards built on automated data may not cover nontechnical controls.
reason: 'Administrative security control' is not a term in the cited sources. SP 800-53 covers training as controls in its AT family (for example AT-2 and AT-3).

value: A is wrong because Special Publication 800-37 names the senior agency official for privacy, not the system owner, as assessor of privacy controls. C provides inheritable controls. D decides on authorisation using the results.
reason: 'Relies on assessors rather than assessing' is hard to follow. The source names the privacy assessor directly: 'The senior agency official for privacy serves as the control assessor for the privacy controls' (SP 800-37, PDF p. 83).
